title: Layout Architect
subtitle: Dense, production-grade pages in one line each

intro.headline: Stop building sections. Start placing them.
intro.body:
Most layout code is people rebuilding the same four things: a page title with actions, a strip of numbers, a filter bar, a board. Aktion ships those as **pattern composites** — one call each, already dense, already responsive, already themed.

Underneath them are the primitives: `Column`, `Row`, `Grid` and a small cast of wrappers. You need them, but you should reach for them *second*. A page hand-composed out of `Card` and `Stack` reads as a wireframe; the same page built from composites reads as a product.

This world is the difference between a screen that validates and a screen that looks finished.
intro.code:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Engineering Q3", { subtitle: "12 active · 4 at risk" }),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true, right: [Button("New project", { variant: "primary" })] }),
  Stats([
    StatCard("Active", { value: "12" }),
    StatCard("At risk", { value: "4", trend: "up", delta: "+2", tone: "warning" })
  ]),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Recent activity"),
    Timeline([TimelineItem("Order #1204 shipped", { time: "2h ago", icon: "truck", tone: "success" })])
  ])
], { gap: "lg" }))

layers.note: the surface the page sits on

layers.label: PageHeader · Stats · Toolbar · KanbanBoard

objectives: Commit a whole page section with one composite call
Make a layout responsive with `{ base, md, lg }` and nothing else
Ship a page dense enough that it looks designed

stages.title: Three primitives, one job each
stages.goal: Pick Column, Row or Grid on reflex — and know the one case that needs Stack.

teach.text:
Three containers do almost all the work. `Column` stacks children top to bottom and stretches them to full width — the default shape of a page body and of a card body. `Row` lays them left to right, keeps every child at its **natural** width, and centres them vertically. `Grid` gives cells that share one width.

`Stack` is the low-level flex box underneath both. Reach for it only when the *direction itself* has to change across breakpoints — because a `row` Stack grows its children equally by default (`uniform` is true for row stacks). Hand it a search field and two buttons and you get three identical thirds.

Spacing is a token, never a pixel: `none · 3xs · 2xs · xs · sm · md · lg · xl · 2xl · 3xl`. The rhythm that reads as designed is `lg` between top-level sections, `md` inside a card, `sm` between tightly related controls.

The rest of the set fills the gaps: `Center` for both-axis centring, `Container` for a readable max width, `Box` when a `Card` is too heavy, `Section` for a full-bleed page band, `Split` for two panes, `Spacer()` to push siblings apart, `Separator` to draw a line.

code.src:
Column([header, kpis, table], { gap: "lg" })

Row([SearchBar("q"), Spacer(), Button("New order")], { gap: "sm" })

Grid(cards, { columns: 4, gap: "md" })
code.caption: top-to-bottom · left-to-right · equal cells

code2.caption: the one job Row and Column cannot do

infographic.title: What people reach for, and what they meant
rows: Row(items, { gap }) — natural widths, vertically centred
Grid(tiles, { columns, gap }) — cells share one width
Row(items) — Column has no direction; it is always vertical
Card([...]) once the chunk is a real page section

tips: `Grid` with no `columns` auto-fits as many equal columns as fit at `minChildWidth` (220px by default) — usually exactly what a KPI wall wants.
Make one child of a `Row` expand with `StackItem(child, { grow: 1 })`; a bare `Spacer()` between two children pushes them to opposite edges.

tips.text: `Column` accepts a `direction` prop the way any object accepts any key — and renders vertically regardless. It is dropped on the floor.

challenge.title: What each call actually renders
challenge.prompt: Five calls, five different shapes on screen. Match each one to what it really puts in front of the user.

right.label: The field at its own natural width, the button shoved to the far right edge
One line, two identical halves — the field comes out as wide as the button
Equal thirds, three across, wrapping onto a new row as the tiles run past three
Two full-width rows stacked vertically — the prop never arrives anywhere
Stacked on a phone, side by side from 768px up

hints: Start with the two that hand every child an identical width — one of them asks for it out loud, the other does it by default.
Only one call in the left column is documented as 'natural width, vertically centred'.
`Spacer()` between two children is what pushes them to opposite edges. A `direction` on a `Column` does nothing at all.
nudges: Ask what each container does to a child's width before you ask what direction it flows in.
One call names a prop its component does not have — and renders exactly as if you had left it off.
stages.explain: `Row` exists precisely so children keep their natural size — a search field stays a search field, a button stays button-sized. `Stack` in `row` mode is the same flex box with `uniform` defaulting to true, which is the whole reason `Row` is a separate component. `Grid(columns: 3)` asks for equal thirds out loud, and `Column` never flows horizontally no matter what you pass it. Same short cast of children, five completely different shapes.

afterCode.src: Row([SearchBar("q"), Spacer(), Button("Filter"), Button("New order", { variant: "primary" })], { gap: "sm" })
afterCode.caption: the shape to remember

codex.def: `Row` keeps children at their natural width and centres them vertically. `Stack(direction: "row")` is the same box with `uniform: true`, stretching every child to an equal share — use it only when the direction must change across breakpoints.

stages.title: One call, one whole section
stages.goal: Reach for a pattern composite before you open a single Card.

teach.text:
Before you compose anything by hand, check whether the library already owns the idiom. `PageHeader` is a page title with breadcrumbs, a status slot and an actions row. `Stats` is a KPI strip. `Toolbar` is a search-and-filters bar. `EmptyState`, `Timeline`, `DescriptionList`, `KanbanBoard`, `FeatureGrid`, `PricingTable`, `Hero`, `SectionHeader` — each of them commits a finished visual section in one line.

They are not shortcuts. They are tuned: spacing rhythm, responsive behaviour, iconography, heading levels and semantic tone all come with them. A hand-rolled equivalent gets none of that and will drift away from every other page in the app.

The rule of thumb for how many sections a page needs: a dashboard wants **six** named sections, a detail, settings, list or landing page wants **five**. Two components stacked vertically is a wireframe, not a product — if a draft is short, add a complementary section rather than padding the ones you have.

code.src:
PageHeader("Orders", { subtitle: "1,204 this month", actions: [Button("Export", { icon: "download" })] })

Toolbar({ searchable: true, right: [Button("New order", { variant: "primary" })] })

Stats([StatCard("Revenue", { value: "$48,120", trend: "up", delta: "+12%" })])

EmptyState("No orders yet", { description: "They land here the moment one arrives." })
code.caption: four sections, four calls

columns.title: Hand-composed
columns.note: Nine lines, no breadcrumbs, no status slot, no heading level — and it will drift from every other page.

columns.title: The composite
columns.note: One call. Breadcrumbs, the status slot and the actions row arrive with it.

tips: `Grid`, `Column` and `Row` still matter — they are the glue *between* composites, not a replacement for them.
`columns`, `gap`, `padding`, `align`, `justify` and `direction` all accept a `{ base, sm, md, lg, xl }` map instead of a value.

challenge.title: Compose the orders page
challenge.prompt: Four nodes are missing from the page tree. Three want the composite that owns that section; the fourth has to survive a 390px phone, so a bare number will not do.

hints: Three of the four slots are pattern composites — each one commits a whole section on its own.
`CardHeader` opens a card. The thing that opens a *page* has a different name.
A responsive prop takes an object keyed by breakpoint: `{ base: …, md: …, lg: … }`.
nudges: Two chips in the bank are the hand-rolled versions of composites already in the bank.
`4` is a legal value for `columns` — it is just wrong for a grid that has to reflow.
stages.explain: Every one of those three composites exists because the same section gets rebuilt on every page of every app. Using them is not laziness — it is how the pages stay consistent with each other, and how you get breadcrumbs, status slots, responsive wrapping and correct heading levels without asking. The `Grid` is the only place a primitive belongs here: it is the glue between the section composites, and a `{ base, md, lg }` map is how it survives a phone.

afterCode.src: Grid(orderCards, { columns: { base: 1, md: 2, lg: 4 }, gap: "lg" })
afterCode.caption: one column on a phone, four on a desktop

codex.def: An opinionated component that commits a whole visual section in one call — PageHeader, Stats, Toolbar, EmptyState, Timeline, DescriptionList, KanbanBoard, FeatureGrid, PricingTable, Hero. Reach for one before composing the same thing out of Card and Stack.

preview.program:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Orders", { subtitle: "1,204 this month", actions: [Button("Export", { icon: "download", variant: "secondary" })] }),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true, searchPlaceholder: "Search orders…", right: [Button("New order", { variant: "primary", icon: "plus" })] }),

    StatCard("Refunds", { value: "18", trend: "down", delta: "-2%", tone: "warning" }),
    StatCard("Customers", { value: "892", trend: "up", delta: "+8%" })
  ]),
  Grid([

    Card([SectionHeader("Fulfilment", { status: Pill("Live", { tone: "success" }) }), Text("Median 1.4 days")])
  ], { columns: { base: 1, md: 2 }, gap: "lg" }),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Recent activity"),
    Timeline([
      TimelineItem("Order shipped", { time: "2h ago", icon: "truck", tone: "success" }),

stages.title: Two chips and two bands
stages.goal: Choose between components the validator is happy to let you confuse.

teach.text:
Some components are near-identical in the prop table and completely different on screen. The schema validator accepts all of them, so this one is on you.

`Badge` is the **solid, high-attention chip** — "Recommended", "Save 50%", "Most popular". `Pill` is the **soft tinted state label** for the current state of a thing — "SSL active", "pending", "broken". Reach for `Pill` when the text describes *what something is right now*, and `Badge` when it is trying to catch an eye.

`Callout` is a standalone bordered notice that stands on its own between two sections. `CardSection` is a full-bleed tinted band that lives **inside** a `Card`, grouping and colouring part of that card's content edge to edge. If it needs its own border, it is a `Callout`; if it needs to be part of a card, it is a `CardSection`.

The same trap runs through the rest of the library: `Spinner` is a rotating ring for a whole panel, `LoadingDots` a quieter inline pulse. `Buttons` is a gapped row, `ButtonGroup` an edge-to-edge joined control, `SegmentedControl` a single-select pill track. `ActionStripe` is an always-interactive navigation row, `ListItem` a presentational row, `Tile` a grid unit.

code.src:
Badge("Recommended", { tone: "primary" })

Pill("SSL active", { tone: "success" })

Callout("Your trial ends in 3 days", { tone: "warning", description: "Add a card to keep the workspace open." })

Card([
  SectionHeader("Danger zone"),
  CardSection([Text("Deleting this project cannot be undone.")], { tone: "critical" })
])
code.caption: chip, state label, notice, band

rows.label: Callout
rows.note: bordered notice standing on its own

rows.label: CardSection
rows.note: tinted band, edge to edge inside one Card

tips: `Pill` and `CardSection` share an enterprise state vocabulary that `Badge` and `Callout` do not have: `activating`, `critical`, `promoting`, `corporate` (alongside the usual `neutral`, `success`, `warning`).

tips.text: `Callout` lists `tone` first in its signature — `Callout(tone, title, …)` — but the argument tagged *positional* is `title`. So `Callout("Trial ends", { tone: "warning" })` is the call you want; never rely on position for the tone.

challenge.title: File each job under its component
challenge.prompt: Eight jobs, four components that all render coloured text on a tinted background. Drop each job on the one that owns it.

bins.label: CardSection
bins.hint: full-bleed tinted band inside a Card

items.label: A bordered "Your trial ends in 3 days" notice between two sections
A dismissible "This cannot be undone" alert on its own
An edge-to-edge red strip closing the settings card
A tinted "Activating…" band grouping three rows of one card

hints: Two of the four are chips you drop inline. Two of them are whole bands.
Ask of every chip: is this the *state of a thing*, or is it shouting for attention?
One of the four can only ever exist inside a `Card`.
nudges: "pending" and "SSL active" describe what something currently is. That is one specific component.
If the notice has its own border and sits between sections, it is not part of any card.
stages.explain: None of these four is a styling variant of the others — they encode *how much attention the thing deserves* and *where it structurally belongs*. Get it wrong and the page still renders and still validates; it just reads wrong, because a solid `Badge` on every row's status turns a calm table into a fairground. Passing `tone`, never a colour, is what lets all four re-skin themselves across the six built-in themes.

codex.def: `Badge` is the solid, high-attention chip ("Recommended", "Save 50%"). `Pill` is the soft tinted label for the current state of a thing ("SSL active", "pending"), with the extra tones `activating`, `critical`, `promoting`, `corporate`.

preview.program:
$app(Column([
  SectionHeader("Two chips and two bands", { eyebrow: "near neighbours" }),
  Row([
    Badge("Recommended", { tone: "primary" }),
    Badge("Save 50%", { tone: "danger" }),
    Pill("SSL active", { tone: "success" }),
    Pill("pending", { tone: "warning" })
  ], { gap: "sm", wrap: true }),
  Callout("Your trial ends in 3 days", { tone: "warning", description: "A standalone bordered notice — it stands on its own between two sections." }),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Danger zone"),
    Text("Normal card content sits here."),
    CardSection([Text("Deleting this project cannot be undone.")], { tone: "critical" })
  ])
], { gap: "lg" }))

stages.title: Blueprint
stages.goal: Fill every region of a dashboard with the composite that finishes it.

teach.text:
A dashboard wireframe is on the table. One region lights up at a time and tells you what it needs.

**Tap the composite that owns that job** before the bar runs out. Get it right and the region fills in dense — a heading bar, a body, a footer rule. Get it wrong, or run out of time, and the region renders as a single thin line: exactly what a page looks like when you hand-compose a section that already exists.

Five filled regions clears the stage. Three sparse ones ends the run.
tips: Read the *job*, not the words. "key / value summary of one record" is a `DescriptionList` even though nothing says list.

tips.text: Two composites are page-level and two are content-level. `PageHeader` never fills a toolbar region, and `Toolbar` never replaces a page header.

challenge.title: Fill the wireframe
challenge.prompt: Each region names what it needs. Tap the one-line composite that fills it before the bar empties.
challenge.note: Tap a composite chip. A wrong pick renders the region visibly sparse — and it stays that way.
challenge.winNote: Press Check to bank the XP.

regions.need: title + breadcrumbs + a right-aligned actions row
four KPIs in one strip, with trend and delta
search + filters + the primary action, above a table
four columns of draggable task cards
a key / value summary of one record
the list came back empty - say so, with a CTA

fallback.prompt: A region above a table needs a search field, two filter chips and one primary action. Which single call fills it?

options.code: Toolbar({ searchable: true, right: [Button("New order", { variant: "primary" })] })
Row([SearchBar("q"), Button("Open"), Button("Paid"), Spacer(), Button("New order")])
options.detail: It renders — it is just the hand-rolled version of a composite that already exists, and it does not wrap onto rows on a narrow viewport the way Toolbar does.
PageHeader is the page title block. It never replaces a Toolbar, and a Toolbar never replaces it.
Navbar is site-level navigation for a marketing or docs page, not a filter bar above a table.

hints: Six regions, six composites, one each — nothing is used twice.
"four KPIs in one strip" is the single most common dashboard section; it has a component named after it.
If a region describes an *absence* of data, there is a composite whose entire job is that.
stages.explain: Every wrong pick left a region that renders a single line — which is exactly what a hand-composed section looks like next to a composite one. The reason the density targets in the skill exist (six sections for a dashboard, five for a detail page) is that a page reads as unfinished long before it reads as broken, and no validator will ever tell you so. The composites are how you hit those targets without writing a hundred lines.

codex.def: The minimum number of named sections a page type needs to read as finished: six for a dashboard, five for a detail, settings, list or landing page, three for a zero state. Short of the target, add a complementary section rather than padding the ones you have.

stages.title: One layout, every viewport
stages.goal: Read a breakpoint map the way the runtime does — which props take one, and where each key takes over.

teach.text:
There is no breakpoint prop, no media-query escape hatch and no mobile variant of any component. Six layout props take a **map** wherever they take a value: `gap`, `padding`, `align`, `justify`, `columns` and `direction`.

The keys are `base`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` — 640, 768, 1024 and 1280 pixels, with `base` as the mobile-first floor. Values cascade upwards, so a breakpoint you leave out inherits the one below it: `{ base: 1, lg: 4 }` is one column all the way to 1024px and four beyond it.

This is where `Stack` finally earns its place. It is the only primitive whose `direction` you can map, which is why a filter rail that becomes a top strip on a phone is a `Stack` and not a `Row`.

code.src: Grid(cards, { columns: { base: 1, md: 2, lg: 4 }, gap: { base: "sm", lg: "lg" } })
code.caption: one column on a phone, four on a desktop

code2.src: Stack([filters, results], { direction: { base: "column", md: "row" }, gap: "lg" })
code2.caption: stacked on a phone, side by side from 768px up

infographic.title: Reading a breakpoint map
infographic.code: Grid(cards, { columns: { base: 1, md: 2, lg: 4 }, gap: "lg" })

parts.text: one of the six props that take a map instead of a value
mobile-first — everything narrower than 640px gets this
takes over at md and holds until the next named key
the widest rule here, so xl inherits it too
a map is per-prop and optional — mix values and maps freely

tips: Leave breakpoints out on purpose. `{ base: 1, lg: 4 }` is usually better than spelling out all five.

tips.text: Unknown breakpoint keys are silently ignored so a typo cannot crash the page. `{ mobile: 1, desktop: 4 }` matches nothing, is treated as a plain value, and quietly gives you the component default.

challenge.title: Four columns, but when?
challenge.prompt: Five Grid calls, all of them legal, all of them asking for four columns. Order them by the viewport width at which each one first actually renders four — narrowest at the top, never at the bottom.

hints: Two of the five have no breakpoint doing any work at all: one is four columns at every width, the other is four columns at none.
`sm` is 640, `md` is 768, `lg` is 1024, `xl` is 1280 — the key names *are* the ladder, and a key you leave out inherits the one below it.
`desktop` is not one of the five keys. Nothing throws; it simply never matches, so `base` holds all the way up.
nudges: Ask of each line: at what width does that `4` first take effect — and does it ever?
A bare `columns: 4` is not a phone layout. It is four columns at 320px too.
stages.explain: The six mappable props are exactly the ones that describe space and arrangement, and the runtime turns each map into real CSS custom properties inside media queries — no JavaScript resize listener, no re-render on rotate. Props that describe what a component *is* rather than how much room it has — `variant`, `size`, or a CSS length like `minChildWidth` — take a single value and nothing else. Each key holds until the next named one takes over, which is why `{ base: 1, xl: 4 }` is one column all the way to 1280px. And because a map is just an object, the runtime cannot tell a typo'd key from a deliberate omission: it ignores what it does not recognise. That is the whole story of the last line: `base` matches and `desktop` does not, so the grid holds one column at 4K exactly as calmly as it does at 320px.

afterCode.src: Stack([filters, results], { direction: { base: "column", md: "row" }, gap: { base: "sm", lg: "lg" } })
afterCode.caption: two maps, zero media queries

codex.def: `{ base, sm, md, lg, xl }` (640/768/1024/1280px) accepted by `gap`, `padding`, `align`, `justify`, `columns` and `direction`. Values cascade upwards; unrecognised keys are silently ignored.

stages.title: Ship something dense
stages.goal: Write a page with five named sections and not one hard-coded colour.

teach.text:
Two habits separate a page that looks designed from one that looks generated.

**Do not fight the defaults.** These components already guess the obvious: `StatCard("Revenue", …)` picks an icon from the label, `PageHeader(title)` derives `["Home", title]` breadcrumbs (pass `breadcrumbs: false` to suppress them), `EmptyState(title)` picks an icon from the title, `Banner(title, { tone })` picks one from the tone, and `Image(src, { ratio: "16:9" })` constrains itself with no outer `AspectRatio`. Passing what they already infer adds noise, not control.

**Never hard-code colour, spacing or typography.** Pass a semantic `tone` or `variant` — `default`, `primary`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, `info` — and let the theme resolve it. The same program has to survive six built-in themes; a hex value survives none of them. (`tone` and `variant` are interchangeable on 41 component specs, and `children`/`child` on 57, so a plausible guess is rarely a build failure.)

Now build one. Five named sections, all of it hanging off a single `$app(...)`.

code.src:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("…"),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true }),
  Stats([StatCard("…", { value: "…" }), StatCard("…", { value: "…" })]),
  Card([SectionHeader("…"), Timeline([TimelineItem("…", { time: "…" })])])
], { gap: "lg" }))
code.caption: the shape, not the answer

infographic.title: The six sections of a dashboard

tips: `SectionHeader` opens a section *inside* a Card; `PageHeader` opens the page. Using the second one twice is the fastest way to make a page look wrong.
If the language service is reachable, its real diagnostics appear under the editor as you type.

challenge.title: Write the console page
challenge.prompt: Write a project console in one `Column`: a `PageHeader`, a `Toolbar`, a `Stats` strip holding at least two `StatCard`s, and a `Card` containing a `SectionHeader` and a `Timeline`. Pass `tone` / `variant` for emphasis — never a colour.
challenge.solution:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Project console", { subtitle: "12 active · 4 at risk" }),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true, searchPlaceholder: "Search projects…", right: [Button("New project", { variant: "primary", icon: "plus" })] }),
  Stats([
    StatCard("Active", { value: "12", trend: "flat" }),
    StatCard("At risk", { value: "4", trend: "up", delta: "+2", tone: "warning" }),
    StatCard("Shipped", { value: "8", trend: "up", delta: "+3", tone: "success" })
  ]),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Recent activity", { status: Pill("Live", { tone: "success" }) }),
    Timeline([
      TimelineItem("Auth migration merged", { time: "2h ago", icon: "shield", tone: "success" }),
      TimelineItem("Mobile onboarding blocked", { time: "5h ago", icon: "triangle-exclamation", tone: "warning" })
    ])
  ])
], { gap: "lg" }))

mustWhy: The sections need a Column([ ... ]) to stack them.
Open the page with a PageHeader.
Add a Toolbar for search and the primary action.
Stats needs at least two StatCard entries.
Open the card with a SectionHeader, not a second PageHeader.
Close with a Timeline([ ... ]) inside that Card.

hints: Start from the outside in: `$app(Column([ … ], { gap: "lg" }))`, then drop one section per line.
`Stats` takes an array of `StatCard(label, { value })` — the icons pick themselves from the labels.
`Card([SectionHeader("Recent activity"), Timeline([TimelineItem("…", { time: "2h ago" })])])` is the last section.
nudges: Every section is one call. If a line is getting long, it is probably the options object, not the structure.
Emphasis is `tone: "warning"` or `variant: "primary"`. If a hex value appears, the theme has lost.
stages.explain: Five sections, one root, and nothing in it that would break if the host switched to the `corporate` or `glass` theme tomorrow. Notice what you did not have to write: no breadcrumb markup, no icon choices, no grid maths for the KPI strip, no media queries, and no colours. That is the whole trade — the composites own the visual decisions so your program only has to say what the page is about.

codex.def: Emphasis is expressed with the semantic palette (`default`, `primary`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, `info`) through `tone` or `variant`, never as a colour, spacing or font value — so one program renders correctly on all six built-in themes.

preview.program:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Project console", { subtitle: "12 active · 4 at risk", status: Badge("On track", { tone: "success" }) }),
  Toolbar({ searchable: true, searchPlaceholder: "Search projects…", right: [Button("New project", { variant: "primary", icon: "plus" })] }),
  Stats([
    StatCard("Active", { value: "12", trend: "flat" }),
    StatCard("At risk", { value: "4", trend: "up", delta: "+2", tone: "warning" }),
    StatCard("Shipped", { value: "8", trend: "up", delta: "+3", tone: "success" })
  ]),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Recent activity", { status: Pill("Live", { tone: "success" }) }),
    Timeline([
      TimelineItem("Auth migration merged", { time: "2h ago", icon: "shield", tone: "success" }),
      TimelineItem("Mobile onboarding blocked", { time: "5h ago", icon: "triangle-exclamation", tone: "warning" })
    ])
  ])
], { gap: "lg" }))
preview.caption: your page, rendered by the real Aktion runtime

outro.headline: You place sections now, you don't build them
outro.body: Composites first, primitives as glue, tone instead of colour, and a breakpoint map wherever a value used to be. That is every dense page you will ever need to write.
outro.nextHint: Next: Flow Control — where expressions end, statements begin, and `if` refuses to sit on the right of an `=`.
